issues.legal_issue: Market value in a land acquisition must be determined by adjusting comparable sale evidence for the relevant differences between the sale property and the acquired land, and deductions may separately account for land size and development needs.
material_facts: The acquisition included 16 plots, including two very large plots and 14 smaller plots.
The principal comparable sale concerned a 46.30-square-metre property sold for Rs. 270 per square metre in a different locality.

Evidence showed that the acquired land had roads, electricity, water, non-agricultural use and nearby residential and commercial uses, but the area was not fully urbanized and its development had practically stopped because of the dam and expected submergence.
Development had shifted to an area across a river, and the acquired land was to be submerged.
The Reference Court deducted development costs from its valuation; the High Court made deductions that varied according to the size of the acquired plots.
The State challenged the deductions as insufficient, while the claimants argued that separate deductions for size and development were impermissible.
issues.conclusion: The Court determined compensation at Rs. 160 per square metre for the large plots and Rs. 175 per square metre for the small plots. It held that relevant deductions depend on the circumstances of the land and that deductions for the size of the land and for development are not necessarily impermissible when made separately.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed as of the date of the Section 4(1) notification, ordinarily by reference to what an informed willing buyer would pay a willing seller. Comparable sale evidence must be assessed for proximity in time and situation, with adjustments for positive and negative features of the sale property and acquired land; the valuation is not mathematically exact. A small-plot sale may be used for a larger acquisition if appropriate adjustments are made. Deductions for size and development depend on the facts and may be distinct; they are not automatic, and an already developed smaller portion of a larger tract may not warrant a deduction merely because the overall tract is large. The Court relied on Bhagwathula Samanna v. Special Tahsildar, L. Kamalamma v. Land Acquisition Officer, Basavva v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, K.S. Shivadevamma v. Assistant Commissioner, Hasanali Khanbhai & Sons v. State of Gujarat, Land Acquisition Officer v. Nookala Rajamallu, and the cases applying ordinary development deductions; it distinguished The Registrar, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad, on its agricultural-land facts.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_small_plot_sale and acquired_plots_differed_in_size and acquired_area_was_to_be_submerged and development_had_shifted_away

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_small_plot_sale: The court considered a sale of a small plot in a different locality as a comparable transaction.
predicates.acquired_plots_differed_in_size: The acquired land included both very large plots and smaller plots.
predicates.acquired_area_was_to_be_submerged: The acquired land was to be submerged as a result of the public project.
predicates.development_had_shifted_away: Development in the acquired locality had practically stopped and had shifted to another area.

issues.definition: When a land-compensation appeal involves a small-plot comparison, acquired plots of different sizes, submergence, and development shifting away, the comparable sale value is adjusted for the relevant differences in fixing market value.

issues.legal_issue: Interest is payable on statutory solatium that forms part of compensation for acquired land.
material_facts: The claimants had been awarded solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
The High Court refused interest on solatium, relying on Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India.
The claimants challenged that refusal, and the Court considered the Constitution Bench decision in Sunder v. Union of India, which had overruled Prem Nath Kapur.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest on solatium.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(2) provides for solatium as part of the compensation, and the Court applied Sunder v. Union of India, which held that the aggregate compensation under Section 23 attracts interest when payment is delayed and overruled Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India. The Court thereby rejected splitting compensation into components to exclude solatium from interest under the applicable interest provision, including Section 28; the reasoning quoted from Sunder also addresses Section 34.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.solatium_was_awarded: The claimants had been awarded statutory solatium as part of the compensation.
predicates.interest_on_solatium_was_denied_below: The lower court refused to award interest on the solatium component.

issues.definition: When a land-compensation appeal concerns awarded solatium on which the lower court denied interest, interest is payable on that solatium.
